**Surah al-Ra'd**

It is Meccan, except for his saying, "And those who disbelieve will not cease," and his saying, "And those who disbelieve say, 'You are not a messenger.'" [Al-Nahhas narrated in *al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh* from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that Surah al-Ra'd is Meccan. Al-Hasan, Ata' and Qatadah also said so. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn al-Zubayr, that Surah al-Ra'd was revealed in Medina. Jabir ibn Zayd also said so. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is Medinan except for two verses revealed in Mecca; Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated this from Qatadah. The Meccan character of the surah is very clear, whether in the nature of its subject, its manner of presentation, or its general atmosphere, which anyone who lives for a period in the shade of the Qur'an cannot fail to sense. See: *al-Durr al-Manthur* 4/599; *al-Itqan* 1/40–44; *Zad al-Masir* 4/299; *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* 13/2039.] [It has forty-three verses.] [Note: the words in the brackets are missing from manuscript "a".]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿Al-Mar.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: its meaning is, "I am Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing." [See above: 1/58. Also consult *Tafsir al-Tabari* (exegesis of al-Tabari) 1/205–224, 6/149, 12/292–294, 15/9, 16/319–320 (Dar al-Ma'arif edition); *Zad al-Masir* 4/300.]

﴿These are the verses of the Book.﴾ That is: these are the reports which I have related to you. [The verses] of the Torah, the Gospel and the earlier scriptures. ﴿And what has been revealed to you﴾ means: this Qur'an which has been revealed to you ﴿from your Lord is the truth.﴾ That is: it is the truth, so hold fast to it. In this case, the word "alladhi" (which) is in the nominative case as a *mubtada'* (subject), and "al-haqq" (the truth) is its *khabar* (predicate).

It was also said: its position is in the genitive case, meaning: "These are the verses of the Book and the verses of that which has been revealed to you," then he began a new sentence with "al-haqq," meaning: "That is the truth." [On this and its evidence from Arabic, see: *Tafsir al-Tabari* 16/321–322; *al-Bahr al-Muhit* 5/359; *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz* 8/109–110.]

Ibn Abbas said: by "the Book" he meant the Qur'an, and its meaning is: "These are the verses of the Book," meaning the Qur'an. Then He said: "And this Qur'an which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth."

﴿But most people do not believe.﴾ Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca when they said, "Muhammad (ﷺ) says it of his own accord." [It was also said that the intended meaning is the Jews and Christians. The more appropriate view is that it is general, encompassing both these and those. See: *al-Bahr al-Muhit* 5/359.] So He rejected their saying, and then He explained the proofs of His lordship, and the Mighty, the Speaker said: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 2:

﴿Allah is He who raised up the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾ That is: the pillars (sawari), the singular of which is ʿamud, like adim and udum (hide and hides); its plural is also ʿumud, like rasul and rusul (messenger and messengers).

Its meaning is the negation of pillars altogether, and this is the most sound view. That is: there is no support beneath them that props them up, nor any suspension above them that holds them.

Iyas ibn Muawiya said: "The sky is vaulted over the earth like a dome."[[This is also narrated from Qatada. It is supported by His explicit statement in Surah al-Hajj that He is the One who holds the sky from falling upon the earth, in His words: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾. On this view, His words ﴿that you can see﴾ are an emphasis negating such support, meaning: they are raised without pillars as you see them. This is the more perfect expression of power. On this view, the pronoun in His words "that you can see" refers back to "the heavens," and the clause "you can see" is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/325; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/500; Adwa' al-Bayan: 3/77-78; al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/110.]]

It was also said: "that you can see" refers back to the pillars, meaning: they have pillars, but you do not see them.[[This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and from Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, and others. Al-Tabari commented on these two views (16/325): "The most correct of the views is to say what Allah the Exalted said: 'Allah is He who raised up the heavens without pillars that you can see,' so they are raised without pillars that we see, as our Lord, exalted is His praise, said, and there is no report otherwise, nor any proof that obliges acceptance of anything other than this."]] It is claimed that their pillar is the mountain Qaf, which encircles the world, and the sky is over it like a dome.[[The use of the word "zaʿama" (it is claimed) indicates the weakening of this view, for "zaʿam" is the mount of falsehood, as the Arabs say. For this reason, we here cite a valuable statement of the Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, in his tafsir of Surah Qaf (4/222), where he said: "It is narrated from some of the early scholars that they said: 'Qaf is a mountain encircling the entire earth, called the mountain of Qaf.' It seems that this, Allah knows best, is from the fabrications of the Children of Israel which some people took from them, seeing the permissibility of narrating from them what is neither confirmed nor denied. In my view, this and its like are the inventions of some of their heretics, through which they confuse people about their religion, just as hadiths were fabricated against the Prophet ﷺ in this community despite the high standing of its scholars, memorizers and imams. How then with the Children of Israel, given the long span of time, the scarcity of critical memorizers among them, their drinking of wine, and their scholars' distortion of words from their places and alteration of the books and signs of Allah! The Lawgiver only permitted narrating from them in His words: 'Narrate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm,' concerning what reason may permit. As for what reason rejects and what is judged to be false and whose falsehood is strongly suspected, it does not belong to this category. And Allah knows best." Then he said: "Many of the early exegetes, and likewise a large number of later ones, have related from the books of the People of the Book in the interpretation of the Glorious Qur'an, though they have no need of their reports, and to Allah belongs praise and grace." Then he cited a strange report, whose chain is not sound, from Ibn ʿAbbas, narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim al-Razi, concerning the mountain Qaf encircling the earth, and said: "There is a break in the chain of this report." Shaykh Ahmad Shakir has gathered Ibn Kathir's remarks on Israʾiliyyat in ʿUmdat al-Tafsir: 1/14-19.]]

﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾: He rose over it. ﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾: He made them submissive for the benefit of His creation, so they are subjugated. ﴿Each runs﴾: that is, they both run according to what Allah the Mighty and Majestic wills. ﴿For a specified term﴾: that is, until a known time, which is the end of the world. [Ibn ʿAbbas said]: By the specified term He meant their stations and their positions, at which they arrive and do not go beyond. ﴿He arranges the affair﴾: He decrees it alone. ﴿He details the signs﴾: He makes the proofs clear. ﴿That you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾: so that you may be certain of His promise and believe it.

And He it is who spread out the earth (مَدَّ الْأَرْضَ) — He spread it out — and placed in it firm mountains (رَوَاسِيَ), that is, stable mountains; its singular is râsiya. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Abu Qubays was the first mountain placed upon the earth." [[Narrated by al-Qurtubi from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAta': 9/280.]] And rivers (أَنْهَارًا) — and He made rivers in it.

And from all fruits He made in it two pairs (زَوْجَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ) — that is, two kinds: red and yellow, and sweet and sour. He covers the night with the day (يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ) — that is, He clothes the day with the darkness of night, and clothes the night with the light of day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect (يَتَفَكَّرُونَ) — so they may draw inferences. And reflection (التَّفَكُّرُ) is the turning of the heart in seeking the meanings of things.

[[The text enclosed in brackets is omitted from ("ب").]] [[In ("أ"): "والفكر" (wa-l-fikr) instead of "والتَّفَكُّرُ".]]

﴿And in the earth are neighboring tracts﴾ (qit'un mutajawirat), meaning close to one another, some drawn near to others. They differ: this one is good and produces growth, this one is a salt flat (sabakhah) that produces nothing, this one yields little, and that one yields much. ﴿And gardens﴾, meaning orchards, ﴿of grapevines, crops, and palm trees, both clustered and single﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs, and Ya'qub read all of these in the nominative, as a conjunction (ʿatf) with "gardens." The others read them in the genitive, in coordination (nasaq) with "grapevines." Ṣinwan is the plural of ṣinw, which denotes palm trees that share one root.

﴿Single﴾ (ghayru ṣinwan) refers to a palm tree standing alone on its own root. The people of tafsir (the science of Qur'anic interpretation) said: ṣinwan means gathered together, and ghayru ṣinwan means scattered. A parallel in speech is qinwan, the plural of qinw (a cluster of dates). From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) about al-'Abbas: "The paternal uncle of a man is the ṣinw of his father." This is part of a hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah, recorded by Muslim in the Book of Zakat, chapter on hastening zakat and withholding it, no. (983): 2/676-677. See also earlier: 1/154. Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/338-339, with the commentary of Mahmud Shakir.

There is no difference between ṣinwan and qinwan in singular and plural forms except in i'rab (grammatical case endings). The nun in the dual is kasra-ended and not tanwin-ed, while in the plural it takes tanwin.

﴿Watered with one water﴾. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Ya'qub read yusqa with the letter ya', meaning all of that is watered with one water. The others read it with ta' (tusqa), following the words ﴿and gardens﴾ and the later words "some of them over others," where it says ba'duha and not ba'dahu. Water is a thin, fluid body by which every living thing has life.

﴿And We favor some of them over others in fruit﴾, meaning in dates and taste. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read yufaḍḍilu with ya', following the verse ﴿He manages the affair and details the signs﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. The others read it with nun, meaning: "And We favor some of them over others in fruit." A hadith includes [in His words] "And We favor some of them over others in fruit," where He said: "the Faridi (a type of date), the daql (a poor-quality date), the sweet, and the sour." [Recorded by al-Tirmidhi in tafsir: 8/544, who said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith. Zayd ibn Abi Unaysah narrated something like this from al-A'mash. Sayf ibn Muhammad is the brother of 'Ammar ibn Muhammad, and 'Ammar is more reliable than him, and he is the son of the sister of Sufyan al-Thawri." Also recorded by al-Tabari in tafsir: 16/344, and al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr 4/605 also to al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh. "Faridi" is a type of date, and it is probably what is meant by al-Barni, a yellow, round date of sweet taste, the best kind; they said the word "barni" is Persian, arabized. "Daql" is the worst kind of date. See Mahmud Shakir's commentary on al-Tabari: 16/343.]

Mujahid said: "It is like the children of Adam, the righteous and the wicked among them, though their father is one."

Al-Hasan said: "This is a parable God set forth for the hearts of the children of Adam. The meaning is: the earth was one clay in the hand of the Most Merciful, the Mighty and Majestic. He spread it out, and it became neighboring tracts. Then He sends down rain upon it from the sky, so this one brings forth its blossoms, trees, fruit, and plants, and that one brings forth its salt flats, its brine, and its corruption, yet each is watered with one water. Likewise, people were created from Adam, peace be upon him. Thus a reminder descends from the sky, so some hearts soften and become humble, and other hearts harden and become heedless."

Al-Hasan also said: "By God, no one sits with the Qur'an without rising from its company with an increase or a decrease." God said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it adds nothing for the wrongdoers except loss﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. [Al-Tabari: 16/340.]

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, meaning what I have mentioned, ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾.

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾. Al-'ajab (amazement) is a change in the soul upon seeing something that is ordinarily considered unlikely. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Its meaning: if you are amazed at their denial of the afterlife resurrection while they acknowledge the origination of creation [from God, Exalted and Majestic] [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]], then their matter is amazing.

The polytheists used to deny resurrection while acknowledging that God Most High originated creation. It is firmly established in hearts that restoration is easier than origination, so this is the point of amazement.

It was also said: its meaning is: if you are amazed at the polytheists' denial and their taking as gods what neither harms nor benefits, which they worship, even though they have seen from the power of God Most High what He has set forth for them as examples, then their saying is amazing. That is: you should also be amazed at their saying: ﴿When we are dust?﴾ after death, ﴿Shall we indeed be in a new creation?﴾, that is, shall we be restored as a new creation as we were before death.

Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "أَئِذَا" with an interrogative hamzah and "إِنَّا" without it, as a statement. Their opposite reading is by Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir. The same applies to "سُبْحَانَ" in its two places, and to al-Mu'minun and Alif-Lam-Mim al-Sajdah. The rest of the readers (al-Baqun) read both with the interrogative in these places, and in al-Saffat in two places in the same way, except that Abu Ja'far agrees with Nafi' in the beginning of al-Saffat, where he places the interrogative first, and Ya'qub does not make the second one interrogative: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be held to account?﴾ [al-Saffat: 53].

God Most High said: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord; and those are the shackles around their necks﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

The Almighty's saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾. Al-istijal (hastening) means seeking to bring a matter forward before its appointed time. Here "the evil" (al-sayyi'ah) is punishment, and "the good" (al-hasanah) is well-being. The polytheists of Makkah used to seek punishment instead of well-being, mocking the Prophet, and they would say: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment" [al-Anfal: 32].

﴿Indeed, exemplary punishments have already passed before them﴾, meaning that punishments had already befallen the nations before them who disobeyed their Lord and denied their messengers. Al-mathulat is the plural of al-mathulah, with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the tha', like sadaqah and sadaqat [[Al-sadaqat: the dowries of women.]].

﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾.

**Allah knows what every female carries** ﴿اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ مَا تَحْمِلُ كُلُّ أُنْثَى﴾ of a male or a female, whether well-formed or deformed, one or two or more. **﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾** i.e., what they reduce, **﴿and what they increase﴾**.

The people of tafsir (exegesis) said [[See these statements and their sources in: al-Durr al-Manthur 4/608-610; Tafsir al-Tabari 16/359-365. Also read the book "Khalq al-Insan bayn al-Tibb wa'l-Qur'an" (The Creation of Man between Medicine and the Qur'an) by Dr. Muhammad Ali al-Bar, the chapter on the cycle of the wombs, pp. 69-82.]]: **the diminishing of the wombs** is menstruation during pregnancy. If the pregnant woman menstruates, this is a deficiency in the child, because menstrual blood is the child's nourishment in the womb. When she sheds the blood, the nourishment decreases and the child becomes deficient. When she does not menstruate, the child increases and is completed. Thus the deficiency is a deficiency in the child's formation through the loss of blood, and the increase is the completion of its formation through the retention of blood.

It was also said: when she menstruates, the nourishment decreases, and the duration of the pregnancy increases until it completes nine months apparently. If she sees blood for five days, she gives birth after nine months and five days. So the diminishing is in the nourishment, and the increase is in the duration [[These statements in interpreting the verse are based on the premise that a pregnant woman menstruates, which is the view of Malik and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. 'Ata', al-Sha'bi and others said: she does not menstruate. Abu Hanifa also said this, and his evidence is the verse. Ibn 'Abbas said in interpreting the verse: it refers to the menstruation of pregnant women. Similarly it was narrated from 'Ikrimah and Mujahid, and it is the view of 'A'isha, who used to issue fatwas to pregnant women that if they menstruated they should abstain from prayer. The Companions were then numerous, and none of them denied her, so it became like an ijma' (scholarly consensus). Abu Hanifa said: if a pregnant woman menstruated and what she saw of blood was menstruation, then the istibra' (the waiting period to establish a slave-woman is not pregnant) by menstruation would not be valid, and this is a consensus. A report from Malik in the Kitab Muhammad indicates that it is not menstruation. See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 9/286; Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas 4/397-399; Tafsir Ibn 'Atiyya 8/130-131; Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi 3/1110.]].

**Al-Hasan said:** its diminishing (ghaydu-ha) is its shortfall from nine months, and its increase is its exceeding nine months. **It was said:** the diminishing is miscarriage (saqt), and the increase is the completion of formation. The minimum duration of pregnancy is six months, for a child may be born at this period and survive. [[This is derived from the Almighty's words: "And his carrying and weaning is thirty months" (al-Ahqaf 46:15), together with His words: "The mothers shall nurse their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing" (al-Baqarah 2:233). Thus, subtracting the two years of weaning from the thirty months leaves six months for the duration of pregnancy. The statements of physicians agree with this: medicine establishes that the minimum pregnancy after which a child can live is six months. This is why Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "As for the minimum duration of pregnancy, the Shari'ah and nature have both attested that it is six months." See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 9/288; al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-Qayyim p. 339; Khalq al-Insan bayn al-Tibb wa'l-Qur'an by Dr. Muhammad Ali al-Bar pp. 451-452.]]

**They differed concerning its maximum:** some people said its maximum is two years, which is the view of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, held this view. A group of scholars held that its maximum is four years, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Hammad ibn Salamah said: Hahm ibn Hayyan was only named Hahm because he remained in his mother's womb for four years. [[Some Malikis and Ibn Hazm denied that a pregnancy could exceed nine months. Ibn Hazm said: "...It is not permissible for a pregnancy to exceed nine months or be less than six months... Whoever claims that pregnancy and weaning could occur over more than thirty months has spoken falsehood and impossibility and has openly rejected the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." After mentioning a number of reports and stories suggesting that a pregnancy may exceed nine months, he said: "All of these reports are fabricated, going back to someone who is not trusted and whose identity is unknown, and it is not permissible to rule in the religion of Allah, the Exalted, on the basis of such things. Among those reported to have held our view is 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: 'Any man who divorces his wife after she has menstruated once or twice and then stops menstruating, let her wait nine months until her pregnancy becomes clear. If her pregnancy does not become clear within nine months, let her observe the iddah (waiting period) of three months after the nine months, the iddah of a woman who has stopped menstruating.' So 'Umar did not consider a pregnancy to exceed nine months, and this is the view of Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Abu Sulayman, and our companions." Ali (Ibn Hazm) said: "Except that the child may die in its mother's womb and remain there indefinitely until she delivers it in fragments over years. If this is correct, then it is a valid pregnancy, and her iddah does not end until she delivers all of it..." What Ibn Hazm championed is what physicians hold: they do not allow a pregnancy to exceed one month past its due date, otherwise the fetus would die in its mother's womb. They regard anything beyond that as the result of a miscalculation. As for what is related about children born years after conception, or a pregnancy in a woman lasting for years, this is what they call the "false pregnancy" (pseudocyesis), a condition afflicting women who desire children but do not conceive. Their abdomens swell with gas, their monthly cycle stops, and the woman believes she is pregnant despite all laboratory and medical tests confirming she is not. And Allah knows best. See all of this in: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 9/288-289; Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-'Arabi 3/1109; al-Durr al-Manthur 4/609. Compare with: al-Muhalla by Ibn Hazm 10/316-318; Khalq al-Insan bayn al-Tibb wa'l-Qur'an by Dr. Muhammad Ali al-Bar pp. 452-454.]]

**﴿And everything with Him is in measure﴾**, i.e., with a determination and limit that it neither exceeds nor falls short of.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 9–11:**

﴿The Knower of the unseen and the seen, the Great, the Exalted﴾. "Who all things are beneath" (i.e., all things are subordinate to Him). "The Exalted" (al-Muta'ali): the One who is raised above everything by His power.

Shaykh Mahmud Shakir corrected it in al-Tabari to "sadat Sa'd" — it is said "sayyid," "sadah," and "sadat."]] Sa'd and rijalat Bakr.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Angels succeed one another among you, angels by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Fajr prayer and the 'Asr prayer. Then those who spent the night among you ascend, and their Lord asks them—and He is most knowing of them—'How did you leave My servants?' They say: 'We left them while they were praying, and we came to them while they were praying.'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Mawaqit al-Salat, chapter on the virtue of the 'Asr prayer: 2/33, and in Bad' al-Khalq; and Muslim in al-Masajid, chapter on the virtue of the Subh and 'Asr prayers and guarding them, no. (632): 1/439; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 2/226. The Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari (2/34): "al-Qurtubi said: The waw in His saying 'yatʿāqabūn' is the sign of the masculine plural subject according to the dialect of Bal-Harith, who are the ones who say 'akalūnī al-baraghīth' (the fleas ate me). From it is the poet's saying: 'bi-Hawran ya'simna al-saliṭ aqāribuhu' (in Hawran, his relatives press the sesame oil). It is a widespread dialect, and al-Akhfash interpreted by it His saying: 'and they secretly conferred, those who did wrong.' He said: Some grammarians have strained in interpreting it and rejecting it as a substitution, and that is an unnecessary artifice, for that dialect is well known and has a clear basis in analogy..."]].

﴿From before him and from behind him﴾, meaning: from in front of this one who hides by night and the one who goes freely by day, and from behind him: from behind his back. ﴿They guard him by the command of Allah﴾, meaning: by the command of Allah, that is, they guard him by the permission of Allah for as long as the decreed matter has not come; when the decreed matter comes, they leave him. It was also said: "they guard him from the command of Allah," i.e., from what Allah commanded them of guarding him.

Mujahid said: There is no servant except that he has an angel assigned to him, who guards him in his sleep and his wakefulness from the jinn, the humans, and the venomous creatures; there is no thing that comes to him intending him harm except that the angel says, "Behind you!" except a thing for which Allah has permitted, and then it strikes him.

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: Were it not that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has assigned to you angels who ward off from you at your eating, your drinking, and your private parts, the jinn would snatch you away. 'Ikrimah said: The verse is about the rulers and their guards, who guard them from before them and from behind them [[al-Tabari preferred it, because His saying "for him are successive angels" is closer to His saying "and whoever hides by night" than to "knower of the unseen," so it is more deserving of being the subject of mention; and because the meaning is supported by the saying of Allah: "And when Allah intends harm for a people, there is no turning it back" — indicating that they are the ones meant. For He, exalted is His remembrance, mentioned a people who were in disobedience to Him and in suspicion, who hide by night and show themselves by day, and who protect themselves with a guard that guards them and a defense that protects them from the people of His obedience, so that they cannot come between them and what they do of the disobedience of Allah. Then He informed that when Allah, exalted is His remembrance, intends harm for them, their guard will not benefit them, nor will their protection repel it from them." As for Ibn 'Atiyyah, he preferred the first interpretation and said: "On both interpretations, the pronouns do not refer to specific humans." It was also said: the verse concerns the two angels seated on the right and on the left, who record the good deeds and the bad deeds, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left﴾ [Qaf: 17]. Ibn Jurayj said: The meaning of "yahfazunahu" is that they guard his deeds upon him by the command of Allah, namely the good deeds and the bad deeds. It was also said: the pronoun in His saying "lahu" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "lahu mu'aqqibat" means: for Muhammad (ﷺ) there are guards from the Most Merciful, from before him and from behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah [meaning: from the evil of the jinn] and the nocturnal and diurnal visitors [[This interpretation came within the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas to follow, concerning the story of Arbad; see the following note.]].

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: These verses were revealed concerning 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, and their story, as narrated by al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is: 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, both of the Banu 'Amir, came intending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while he was sitting in the mosque with a group of his companions. They entered the mosque, and people looked at 'Amir's beauty—he was one-eyed and was among the most [handsome] [[In "B": "ajmal" (most beautiful).]] of people. A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who has come toward you." He said: "Leave him; if Allah wills good for him, He will guide him."

He came until he stood over him and said: "O Muhammad, what do I get if I embrace Islam?"

He said: "You will have what the Muslims have, and you will bear what the Muslims bear."

He said: "Will you make the affair mine after you?"

He said: "That is not up to me; it is up to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, who places it wherever He wills."

He said: "Then will you make me [ruler] over the wabar (the camel-hair tents) while you are over the madar (the cities)?" He said: "No."

He said: "Then what will you give me?"

He said: "I will give you the reins of horses by which you may raid."

He said: "Is that not mine today? Get up with me and I will speak with you." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) got up with him.

'Amir had instructed Arbad ibn Rabi'ah: "When you see me speaking with him, go behind him and strike him with the sword." So he began disputing with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and arguing with him, and Arbad went behind the Prophet (ﷺ) to strike him, but he drew a hand's breadth of his sword, then Allah the Exalted held him back, so he could not draw it. 'Amir began gesturing to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned, saw Arbad and what he had done with his sword, and said: "O Allah, suffice me against them both however You will." So Allah sent a thunderbolt upon Arbad on a clear, scorching day, and it burned him. 'Amir fled, saying: "O Muhammad, you invoked your Lord and He killed Arbad! By Allah, I will fill it against you with horses, bare-backed, and young men, beardless!"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May Allah keep you from that." And "the sons of Qaylah" he meant: the Aws and the Khazraj. 'Amir alighted at the house of a woman of the Salul tribe. When morning came, he gathered his weapons upon himself, and his color had changed; he began running in the desert, saying: "Come out, O Angel of Death!" and reciting poetry, and saying: "By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, if I see Muhammad and his companion"—meaning the Angel of Death—"I will pierce them both with my spear!" So Allah sent to him an angel, who struck him with his wing and threw him down into the dust, and immediately a great swelling emerged on his knees. He returned to the house of the Salul woman, saying: "A swelling like the swelling of a camel, and death in the house of a Salulite woman!" Then he called for his horse, mounted it, and drove it until he died upon its back. In this story Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed His saying: ﴿It is the same for you whether one of you conceals speech or speaks openly therewith, and whoever hides by night and goes freely by day. For him are successive angels before him and behind him﴾, meaning: for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there are successive angels who guard him from before him and from behind him by the command of Allah [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 16/379–381; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/296; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, pp. 314–315; Ibn Kathir: 2/507. For he made the pronoun in "lahu mu'aqqibat" refer to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though there was no prior mention of him in the verse before it, nor in the one before that, unless he intended to return it to His saying "You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide," and "for him are successive angels." If that is so, it is far-fetched, because of the intervening verses without any mention of the report about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Given that, its referring back to "man" in His saying "and whoever hides by night" is closer, since it precedes it and the report follows it about him. Given that, the meaning of the speech is: It is the same among you—O people—whether one conceals speech or speaks aloud before your Lord, and whoever hides in the darkness of the night his wickedness and suspicion, and whoever goes and comes in the light of day, protected by his army and guard who surround him from the people of Allah's obedience, lest they come between him and what he does of that, and lest they establish the limit of Allah upon him; and that is His saying: "They guard him by the command of Allah." Likewise Ibn 'Atiyyah said in al-Muharrar al-Wajiz (8/137): "Although its wording fits the meaning of the story, the view that the Prophet (ﷺ) had no prior mention, so that the pronoun in 'lahu' would refer to him, is weak."]]. [Meaning those successive angels are by the command of Allah.] There is also inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it.

He said, concerning these two (i.e., those who hide and those who go about): ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people﴾ of well-being and blessing, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾, of good state, so that they disobey their Lord.

﴿And when Allah intends harm for a people﴾, that is, punishment and destruction, ﴿there is no turning it back﴾, that is, there is no one to repel it. ﴿And for them, besides Him, there is no protector﴾, that is, no refuge to which they can flee. It was also said: "wali" means one who takes charge of their affairs and prevents punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 12–13:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope﴾. It was said: a fear of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa), and a hope for the benefit of the rain. It was also said: the fear is for the traveller, who fears from it harm and hardship, and the hope is for the one who stays at home, who hopes from it blessing and benefit.

It was also said: the fear is of rain that falls out of its place and time, and the hope is when it falls in its place and time. Among the lands there are those which, when they are rained upon, suffer drought, and when they are not rained upon, become fertile.

﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ with rain. It is said: Allah produced (anshaa) the cloud, and it arose (nasha'at), meaning He made it appear and it appeared. Al-sahab is a collective noun, its singular being sahaba. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The cloud is the sieve of the water."

﴿And the thunder glorifies Him with His praise﴾. Most of the exegetes hold that "al-Ra'd" (thunder) is the name of an angel who drives the clouds, and the sound heard from it is its glorification (tasbih) [[See what has preceded: 1/69–70.]].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: Whoever hears the sound of thunder and says, "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels from His awe, and He is over all things Powerful," then if a thunderbolt strikes him, I will pay its blood-money (diya).

And from ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr: that when he heard the sound of thunder, he would stop speaking and say, "Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels from His awe," and he would say: "Indeed this warning is severe for the people of the earth" [[See: al-Adhkar of al-Nawawi, p. 154; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/506, where the supplications recited upon hearing the sound of thunder are mentioned.]].

And in some reports Allah the Exalted says: ﴿If My servants had obeyed Me, I would have given them rain by night, and caused the sun to rise upon them by day, and I would not have let them hear the sound of thunder﴾ [[A weak hadith narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in al-Musnad, p. 337, no. 2586, and by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad: 2/359, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Hakim authenticated it in al-Mustadrak: 2/349, but al-Dhahabi criticised him and said: "Sadaqa is weak (wahin)," and he is Sadaqa ibn Musa al-Daqiqi, a truthful narrator who has errors (Taqrib). Ibn al-Jawzi included it in al-ʿIlal al-Mutanahiya: 2/306, and al-Albani declared it weak in his commentary on Mishkat al-Masabih: 3/1461.]] And Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The thunder is an angel appointed over the clouds, turning them wherever he is commanded. The seas of water are in the hollow of his thumb, and he glorifies Allah the Exalted. When he glorifies Him, no angel remains in the sky without raising his voice in glorification, and then the rain descends."

﴿And the angels from His awe﴾: that is, the angels glorify Allah the Mighty and Majestic out of fear and reverence for Him. It was also said: by these angels is meant the helpers of the thunder; Allah the Exalted has appointed helpers for it, and they are fearful, submissive and obedient.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾, the plural of ṣāʿiqa, which is: a destroying punishment that descends from the lightning and burns whoever it strikes. ﴿So He strikes with it whom He wills﴾, as it struck Arbad ibn Rabiʿa. Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Baqir said: the thunderbolt strikes the Muslim and the non-Muslim, but does not strike the one who remembers (Allah).

﴿While they dispute﴾ they quarrel, ﴿concerning Allah﴾. It was revealed concerning Arbad ibn Rabiʿa, when he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Of what is your Lord made? Of pearl, or of ruby, or of gold?" Then a thunderbolt came down from the sky and burned him [[See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/507.]].

Al-Hasan was asked about His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: A man among the tyrants of the Arabs, the Prophet ﷺ sent to him a group calling him to Allah and His Messenger. He said to them: "Tell me about the Lord of this Muhammad to whom you are calling me: of what is He made? Of gold, or silver, or iron, or copper?" The people were appalled by his words, so they returned to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have not seen a man more disbelieving in heart or more insolent towards Allah than him." He said: "Return to him." So they returned to him, and he did not increase them beyond his first statement, and he said: "I will answer Muhammad with a Lord I neither see nor know." They departed and said: "O Messenger of Allah, he has only added to his first statement, and become more evil."

He said: "Return to him." So they returned. While they were with him, disputing with him and calling him, and he was saying this statement, a cloud rose and came to be above their heads, thundered and flashed, and cast a thunderbolt, and the disbeliever was burned while they were sitting there. They came running to inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ met them and said to them: "Your companion has been burned." They said: "How do you know?" They said: "Allah revealed to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts, so He strikes with them whom He wills, while they dispute concerning Allah﴾" [[See: Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, p. 314; al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti: 4/625–626; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/375; Ibn Kathir 2/507. A similar report from Anas was narrated by Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat. The narrators of Abu Ya'la are sound narrators apart from Dillam ibn Ghazwan, who is trustworthy; and among the narrators of Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani is ʿAli ibn Abi Shara, who is weak. See: Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/42.]].

﴿And He is severe in might﴾. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Severe in seizing." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 16/396. Shaykh Mahmud Shakir said: 16/392: "This chain is munkar."]]

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Severe in power (al-hawl)." [[al-Tabari: 16/396.]]

al-Hasan said: "Severe in enmity (al-hiqd)." [[al-Suyuti attributed it to Abu al-Shaykh from ʿIkrima in al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/627. Al-Tabari narrated from ʿIkrima: "What befell Arbad was the thunderbolt." Al-Tabari also narrated from al-Hasan in explaining the verse: "i.e. destruction; he said: when it is a drought, it is severe." I do not think this explanation the author mentions is correctly attributed to al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, since we found the opposite in al-Tabari, and Allah the Exalted is not fitting to be described by this. And Allah knows best.]]

Mujahid said: "Severe in strength" [[See al-Tabari: the previous reference.]].

Abu ʿUbayda said: [188b] "Severe in punishment."

It was also said: "Severe in plotting."

And al-mihal and al-muhalaha: contending in cunning and overpowering.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 14:

﴿To Him is the true call﴾, i.e., to Allah belongs the call of truth (al-sidq).

ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The true call is the Oneness of God (al-tawhid)" [[al-Tabari: 16/398.]].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah" [[al-Tabari: 16/398.]].

It was also said: it is the supplication made with sincerity (al-ikhlas), and sincere supplication is only directed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic [[These meanings are all close to one another, and there is no contradiction among them.]].

﴿And those who call upon other than Him﴾, i.e., those who worship idols besides Allah, the Exalted.

﴿will not respond to them with anything﴾, i.e., they do not answer them with anything they desire of benefit or of averting harm, ﴿except like one who extends his hands toward the water to reach his mouth, but it will not reach it﴾.

Meaning: except like one who extends his hands to grasp water, while nothing is in his hand and none of the water reaches his mouth. Likewise is the one who calls upon idols, which neither harm nor benefit, and nothing is in their hands.

It was also said: its meaning is like the thirsty man who sees water from afar, points with his palm toward the water and calls to it with his tongue, but it never comes to him. This is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid.

Similar to this is what is reported from ʿAli and ʿAta: like the thirsty man sitting on the edge (shafir) of a well, stretching his hand toward the well, yet he cannot reach the water at the bottom, and the water does not rise up to him. Spreading his palm toward the water and calling to it does not benefit him, and it does not reach his mouth. Likewise, those who call upon idols gain nothing from calling upon them, for they have no power over anything.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: like the thirsty man who spreads his palms in the water; this does not benefit him unless he scoops the water with them, and the water does not reach his mouth as long as he keeps his palms spread. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers﴾ to their idols, ﴿is nothing but in error﴾, that which strays from them when they are in need of it, as He said: ﴿and what they used to fabricate has strayed from them﴾ (al-An'am 24, and elsewhere).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 15:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿To Allah prostrate whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ means: the angels and the believers. ﴿Unwillingly﴾ means: the hypocrites and the disbelievers who were compelled to prostrate by the sword.

﴿And their shadows﴾ means: the shadows of those who prostrate, willingly and unwillingly, prostrate to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willingly. Mujahid said: the shadow of the believer prostrates willingly while he is obedient, and the shadow of the disbeliever prostrates willingly while he is unwilling.

﴿In the mornings and the evenings﴾ means: when he prostrates in the morning or the evening, his shadow prostrates along with him. "Al-asal" (the evenings) is the plural of "al-usul," and "al-usul" is the plural of "al-asil," which is the period from the afternoon prayer until the sunset.

It has also been said: "their shadows" means their persons (ashkhas), "in the mornings and the evenings" means in the early hours and the late afternoons. It has also been said: the prostration of the shadow is its submission to what it has been made for.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 16:

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?﴾ meaning: their Creator and their Governor. [﴿Then they will say: Allah﴾] [[The text between the brackets is omitted from manuscript "B".]] because they acknowledge that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of the heavens and the earth. So when they answer you, then you say too, O Muhammad: "Allah." It is narrated that when he said this to the polytheists, they turned on him and said: "You answer." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him, and he said: ﴿Say: Allah﴾.

Then Allah said to them, as a means of establishing the proof against them: ﴿Say: Have you then taken besides Him protectors who do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm?﴾ Its meaning: even though you affirm that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, you have taken besides Him protectors and worshipped them besides Allah, meaning: the idols, and they ﴿do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm﴾. So how could they possess [anything] for you?

Then He set forth for them a parable, saying: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ Likewise, the disbeliever and the believer are not equal. ﴿Or are the darknesses and the light equal?﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read "yastawi" with a *ya'* (the verb is in the masculine form), while the others read it with a *ta'* (feminine form), because there is no barrier between the noun and the feminine verb.

﴿The darknesses and the light﴾: meaning, just as darkness and light are not equal, disbelief and faith are not equal.

﴿Or have they set up partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ Meaning: they set up partners, ﴿who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed alike to them﴾, i.e., what they created became confused with what Allah Most High created, so they do not know what is the creation of Allah and what is the creation of their gods.

﴿Say: Allah is the Creator of everything, and He is the One, the Irresistible.﴾ Then Allah Most High set forth two parables for truth and falsehood, saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿He sends down﴾, meaning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿water from the sky﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and valleys flow﴾ with that water ﴿each according to its measure﴾, that is, in their smallness and their largeness. ﴿So the torrent carries﴾ from that water ﴿a foam that rises﴾. The foam (zabad) is the scum that appears on the surface of water, and likewise on the surface of a cooking pot. "Rabiyan" means high, raised above the water. So the clear water that remains is the truth, while what departs and vanishes, clinging to the trees and the sides of the valleys, is falsehood.

It has also been said: His words, ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, are a parable for the Qur'an, and the valleys are a parable for hearts. The meaning is: He sends down the Qur'an, and hearts carry from it according to the measure of their certainty, their intellect, their doubt and their ignorance. This is one of the two parables. The other parable is His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And from that which they heat in the fire﴾.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿yūqidūna﴾ with the letter ya', because of His words ﴿what benefits people﴾, and there is no direct address here. The others read it with ta' ("tūqidūna"), meaning: and from that which you heat in the fire. Al-iqad (kindling) is placing fire beneath a thing so that it melts.

﴿Seeking ornament﴾, that is, seeking adornment, and he means gold and silver, because ornaments are sought from them. ﴿Or goods﴾, that is, seeking goods, which is what is useful, such as iron, copper, lead and brass, which are melted so that vessels and other useful things are made from them. ﴿There is a foam like it.﴾

﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and falsehood﴾: that is, when these are melted, they too have a foam like the foam of water. The clear remainder of these substances is like the truth, and the foam that is of no benefit is like falsehood.

﴿As for the foam﴾ that rises above the torrent and the molten metal, ﴿it passes away as scum﴾, that is, lost and vain. The scum (jufa') is what the valley casts out of foam, and what the pot casts to its sides. It is said: the valley "jafa" and "ajfa'a" when it casts out its debris; and the pot "ajfa'at" and "jafa'at" when it boils and casts out its foam. When it settles, nothing remains in it.

Its meaning: falsehood, even if it rises for a time, will vanish. It has also been said: "jufa'an" means scattered, as it is said: the wind "jafa'at" the clouds when it scatters them and carries them away.

﴿As for what benefits people﴾, meaning the water and the molten metal of gold, silver, brass and copper, ﴿it remains in the earth﴾, that is, it endures and does not vanish.

﴿Thus Allah strikes the parables﴾. Allah, exalted, made this a parable for truth and falsehood: falsehood is like foam that passes away and is lost, and truth is like water and molten metal that remains in hearts. It has also been said: this is a consolation for the believers, meaning that the affair of the polytheists is like foam, which appears in form as something but has no reality, while the affair of the believers is like water settled in its place, which has endurance and stability.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 18–19:

Allah's saying: ﴿For those who respond to their Lord﴾ — they responded to their Lord and obeyed Him. ﴿The best [reward]﴾ — Paradise. ﴿But those who do not respond to Him, even if they had all that is in the earth entirely and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom﴾ — meaning, they would expend all of that on the Day of Resurrection to ransom themselves from the Fire. ﴿For those is the evil of the reckoning﴾. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "The evil of the reckoning is that a man is called to account for all his sins, and nothing of them is forgiven him." ﴿And their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾ — the bed; meaning, wretched is what has been prepared for them.

Allah's saying: ﴿Is then one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾ — i.e., one who believes in it and acts by what is in it, versus one who is blind to it, neither knowing it nor acting upon it. It was said: this was revealed concerning Hamzah and Abu Jahl. It was also said: concerning 'Ammar and Abu Jahl. [[Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned this in al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/160, then said: "And it is, after this, an example for all of humanity."]]

﴿Seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾ desiring to glorify Him by not opposing Him.

Al-Qutaybi said: its meaning is: when they are met with foolishness, they respond with forbearance. So "foolishness" is the evil deed, and "forbearance" is the good deed.

Qatadah said: they return kindness to them. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63].

Al-Hasan said: when they are deprived, they give; when they are wronged, they pardon; and when they are cut off, they maintain ties.

'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: "These are eight qualities, pointing to the eight gates of Paradise."

﴿Those will have the good final abode﴾ meaning Paradise; that is, their ultimate end is the abode of reward. Then He explained this, saying: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 23:

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence (jannat 'adn)﴾, i.e., gardens of abiding (bisatin iqamah), ﴿which they will enter, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. The angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾.

It is said: from the gates of Paradise. And it is said: from the gates of the palaces.

﴿Peace be upon you﴾, that is, they say: "Peace be upon you."

It was also said: they say, "May God protect you from the calamities you used to fear."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verses 26–28:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills, and restricts it.﴾ That is: He widens it for whomever He wills and constricts it for whomever He wills.

﴿And they rejoice in the worldly life.﴾ That is: the polytheists of Makkah became exultant and insolent. Joy (al-faraḥ, a pleasure in the heart at attaining what one desires). In it is evidence that rejoicing in this world is forbidden.

﴿Yet the worldly life, in comparison with the Hereafter, is but a brief enjoyment.﴾ That is: little and passing away. Al-Kalbi said: it is like the small dish (sukurrujah), the platter, the bowl and the cooking pot, which are used for a while [then pass away].

﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾ from among the people of Makkah, ﴿"Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance."﴾ [That is: He guides to Himself whoever He wills through turning in repentance. It was also said: He guides to His religion whoever turns to Him with his heart.]

﴿Those who believe﴾ is in the accusative position, a substitute (badal) for "whoever turns back." ﴿And whose hearts find rest﴾ means: are at peace. ﴿In the remembrance of Allah﴾ Muqatil said: in the Qur'an. Tranquility comes through certainty, and agitation comes through doubt. ﴿Surely in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.﴾ The hearts of the believers are calmed and certainty settles within them.

Ibn Abbas said: this concerns oaths. He means: when a Muslim swears by Allah concerning something, the hearts of the believers are at rest with it.

If it is asked: Did not Allah, the Exalted, say: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾ [al-Anfal: 2]? How, then, can tranquility and trembling exist in one state? It is answered: trembling occurs when the threat and punishment are mentioned, and tranquility occurs when the promise and reward are mentioned. Hearts tremble when they recall the justice of Allah and the severity of His reckoning, and they find rest when they recall the bounty of Allah, His reward and His generosity.

The verse: ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿tuba for them﴾ is the predicate (khabar).

The scholars differed over the meaning of ﴿tuba﴾ [[See the discussion of the meaning of tuba and its narrations in al-Tabari: 16/434-444, and al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/642-643.]].

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it means joy for them and comfort of the eye.

'Ikrimah said: it means a excellent wealth for them.

Qatadah said: it means a good end for them.

Ma'mar related from Qatadah: this is an Arabic word. A man says to another, "Tuba laka," meaning, "You have obtained good."

Ibrahim said: it means good for them and honour.

Al-Farra' said: [its root is from al-tayyib (the good), and the waw in it is due to the damma on the ta'. It has two forms. The Arabs say, "Tubaka" and "Tuba laka," meaning, "For them is the good."] [[The text between the brackets is missing from manuscript "B".]].

﴿And a good return﴾ means a good place of return.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas: Tuba is the name of Paradise in Abyssinian (Habashi) language.

Al-Rabi' said: it is the garden in the language of India.

It is related from Abu Umamah, Abu Hurayrah and Abu al-Darda', who said: [Tuba is a tree in Paradise whose shade covers all the gardens. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said] [[The text between the brackets is missing from manuscript "B".]]: it is a tree in the Garden of Eden, its root is in the house of the Prophet ﷺ, and in every house and chamber there is a branch of it. Allah has not created any colour or flower except that it is in it, except black, and Allah the Exalted has not created any fruit or produce except that it is in it. Two springs gush from its root: al-Kafur and al-Salsabil.

Muqatil said: every leaf of it shelters a nation, and on it is an angel glorifying Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with various kinds of glorification [[These narrations, and others like them, contain many additions beyond the sound hadith that will come in the explanation of "tuba," and they contain much exaggeration. Al-Tabari transmitted them, and the Hafiz Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, criticised some of them. These narrations are from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives taken from Jewish and Christian sources). Sufficient for us in the explanation of "tuba" is the sound, agreed-upon hadith that the author transmitted from the narration of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him. See: al-Isra'iliyyat wa al-Mawdu'at by Abu Shahbah, pp. 323-326. Ibn 'Atiyyah, in al-Muharrar al-Wajiz: 8/168, pointed to those narrations and exaggerations, whose implication is that this tree is not in any house of Paradise without some of its branches being in it, that it produces the garments of the people of Paradise, and that from it come horses with their saddles and bridles... and similar things whose chain of transmission is not established.]].

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "What is Tuba?" He said: "A tree in Paradise, a journey of a hundred years, the garments of the people of Paradise come out of its sheaths."[[Transmitted by al-Tabari: 16/443-444, and Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad: 3/71, and Ibn Hibban, no. **The Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 13, Verse 30:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿Thus We have sent you to a community﴾: just as We sent the prophets to their peoples, We have sent you to this community. ﴿Before it, communities have passed away﴾: they have gone. ﴿So that you might recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾: "so that you might recite" means "so that you might read."

Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj said: The verse is Medinan. It was revealed concerning the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah. When Suhayl ibn Amr came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and they agreed to write the treaty document, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Write, 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.'" They said: "We do not know the Most Merciful except the lord of al-Yamamah," meaning Musaylimah the Liar. "Write as you used to write: 'In Your name, O Allah.'" This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾. [[Narrated by al-Tabari, vol. 16, pp. 445–446. al-Suyuti attributed it also to Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh from Qatadah, and to Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn Jurayj. See: al-Durr al-Manthur, vol. 4, p. 650; Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 315; al-Qurtubi, vol. 9, pp. 317–318; al-Bahr al-Muhit, vol. 5, p. 390.]]

However, the well-known view is that the verse is Meccan, and its occasion of revelation was that Abu Jahl heard the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in al-Hijr supplicating, "O Allah, O Most Merciful." He returned to the polytheists and said: "Muhammad supplicates two gods: he supplicates Allah, and he supplicates another god called the Most Merciful, and we do not know the Most Merciful except the Most Merciful of al-Yamamah." Then this verse was revealed, and there was also revealed His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra: 110]. [[See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi, vol. 9, p. 318, and vol. 13, p. 64; al-Bahr al-Muhit, vol. 5, p. 390.]]

al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Prostrate to the Most Merciful." They said: "And what is the Most Merciful?" [[See: Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 315; al-Qurtubi, vol. 9, p. 318; al-Bahr al-Muhit, vol. 5, p. 390.]] Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say﴾ to them, O Muhammad: "Indeed, the Most Merciful, whose knowledge you have denied, ﴿He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. Upon Him I have relied﴾, I have depended, ﴿and to Him is my return﴾," meaning: my repentance and my final return.

The Qur'anic verse: **"And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion, or the earth were split asunder by it, or the dead were made to speak by it..."** (13:31). The passage begins with the Qur'an's words quoted in full.

God's words, may He be exalted and glorified: **"And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion..."**, to the end of the verse. It was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists of Makkah, among them Abu Jahl ibn Hisham and Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah. They sat behind the Ka'bah and sent for the Prophet (ﷺ), and he came to them. Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said to him: "If it would please you that we follow you, then set the mountains of Makkah in motion by the Qur'an and remove them from us until the land opens up, for it is a narrow land for our farms. Make for us springs and rivers in it so that we may plant trees, sow, and make gardens. You are not, as you claim, any more honoured by your Lord than Dawud (peace be upon him), to whom He subjected the mountains, which glorified God along with him. Or subject the wind to us so that we may ride it to Syria for our provisions and needs and return the same day, for the wind was subjected to Sulayman, as you claim. You are not more honoured by your Lord than Sulayman. And bring back to life for us your grandfather Qusayy, or whichever of our forefathers and dead you wish, so that we may ask him about your matter: is what you say true or false? For Isa (Jesus) used to raise the dead, and you are not more honoured by God than he." Then God, may He be exalted and glorified, revealed: **"And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were set in motion..."** [[See al-Tabari: 16/449–450; Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 316; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/318; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/391; al-Durr al-Manthur: 4/651–653; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 2/416.]] and so they were removed from the surface of the earth. **"Or the earth were split asunder by it"**, meaning it was cleft and made into rivers and springs. **"Or the dead were made to speak by it."**

Scholars differed over the answer (jawab) to *law* ("if", لَوْ):

Some said its answer is omitted, the listeners being left to understand its meaning, and its implied sense is: "this Qur'an would have been..." as in the words of the poet: [[This is Imru' al-Qays; the verse is in his Diwan, p. 113. See also al-Tabari: 15/277, 16/448.]]

"By God, if any messenger had come to us other than you,
But we have found no way to repel you."

He meant: "we would have rejected it." This is the meaning of Qatadah's statement, who said: "If this had been done with a Qur'an before your Qur'an, it would have been done with your Qur'an."

Others said the answer to *law* is placed before it, and the sense of the speech is: **"And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful"** [[See al-Tabari: 16/446–447; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/391.]] as if He had said: "Even if the mountains were set in motion by it, or the earth were split asunder by it, or the dead were made to speak by it, they would still disbelieve in the Most Merciful and would not believe, because of what has already preceded in Our knowledge concerning them," as He said: **"Even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them and We had gathered before them all things, they would not have believed"** (6:111). Then He said:

**"Rather, to God belongs the whole affair."** That is: concerning these things, if He wills He does them, and if He wills He does not.

**"Have not those who believe despaired?"** Most of the commentators (mufassirun) said its meaning is: "Have they not known?" Al-Kalbi said: "It is the dialect (lughah) of al-Nakha'."

It was also said: it is the dialect of Hawazin, and this is indicated by the reading of Ibn Abbas: "Have not those who believe made clear (yatabayyan)?" [[al-Tabari: 16/451.]]

Al-Farra' denied that this word has the meaning of "knowing," and claimed that he had not heard any Arab say "yi'istu" meaning "I knew," but that the sense of knowing is implied in it. [[See al-Tabari: 16/451–452. Al-Tabari preferred the first view, which al-Baghawi attributes to most of the mufassirun, saying (16/455): "The correct view on this matter is what the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said, that its interpretation is: 'Have they not made clear and known,' by the consensus (ijma') of the people of interpretation on this. So the sense of the speech is: 'Even if another Qur'an besides this Qur'an had the mountains set in motion by it, it would have set them in motion by this Qur'an; or the earth were split by it, it would have split by this; or the dead were made to speak by it, it would have made them speak by this. But it was not done with a Qur'an before this Qur'an, so that it would be done with this one.' 'Rather, to God belongs the whole affair': He says: all of that is up to Him and in His hand. He guides whom He wills to faith and grants him success in it, and He leaves astray whom He wills and forsakes him. Have not those who believed in God and His Messenger made clear, when they hoped for my answer to the one who asked their prophet for what he asked of him, namely the moving of the mountains away from them, the bringing near of the land of Syria to them, and the bringing back to life of their dead, that if God willed He could guide all people to faith in Him without any sign being produced or anything they asked to be produced? He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: what is the meaning of their desire for that, when they know that guidance and destruction are up to Me and in My hand, whether I send down a sign or not? I guide whom I will without sending down a sign, and I lead astray whom I will even when a sign is sent down.']]

The reason for this is that when the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard this from the polytheists, they hoped that God would do what they asked so that they would believe. So this was revealed: **"Have not those who believe despaired?"** meaning the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, regarding the faith of these people; that is, they did not despair in knowledge. Whoever knows something has despaired of its opposite. It is said: "Did not knowledge make them despair?" **"That if God willed, He would have guided all people."**

**"And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve, for what they have done"** of their disbelief and their wicked deeds, **"a calamity (qari'ah)"**, that is, an event and a great affliction striking them with various kinds of trials: sometimes with drought, sometimes with plunder, sometimes with killing and captivity.

Ibn Abbas said: by the *qari'ah* he meant the expeditions (sara'ya) which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to send against them.

**"Or it settles close to their home"**, meaning the expedition and the calamity. It was also said: "or settles" means that you yourself, O Muhammad, would descend close to their dwellings. **"Until the promise of God comes."** It was said: this is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the conquest, the victory, and the triumph of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his religion.

**"Indeed, God does not fail in His promise."** The disbelievers used to ask for these things in mockery, so God revealed, as consolation for His Prophet (ﷺ): **"And messengers before you were certainly mocked"** (13:32).

﴿Indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾, just as you are mocked, ﴿so I granted respite to those who disbelieved﴾, I gave them time and prolonged their term. From this comes the word "al-malawan" (the two long periods, i.e., night and day). ﴿Then I seized them﴾, I punished them in this world by killing and in the Hereafter by the Fire. ﴿So how was My punishment?﴾, that is, My punishment of them.

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Him]?﴾ That is, the One who watches over it, provides for it, knows it, and recompenses it for what it has done. Its answer is omitted, and its estimated meaning is: "like one who does not stand over anything, but is incapable even of himself."

﴿And they ascribe to Allah partners. Say: Name them﴾, that is, specify their names.

It is also said: describe them, then consider whether they deserve to be worshipped.

﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know on the earth﴾, that is, do you inform Allah, exalted is He, of what He does not know? For He knows of no partner for Himself, and there is no god on the earth other than Him. ﴿Or [do you rely on] an apparent [saying]﴾, meaning: do you rely on an apparent ﴿saying﴾ that is heard, which in reality is false and has no basis?

It is also said: [do you rely on] a false saying. The poet said:

That is, it has departed. [[Abu Mansur said in Tahdhib al-Lughah: "Al-shakah" is used in place of blame and censure. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 13, verse 37–38:

﴿And thus We have sent it down as a judgment in Arabic.﴾ He says: Just as We sent down the Book to you, O Muhammad, and the factions (al-ahzab) denied it, so too We sent down the judgment (al-hukm) and the religion (al-din) in Arabic. It is ascribed to the Arabs because it was revealed in their language, yet the factions denied it. It was also said: the construction of the verse is: just as Books were sent down to the Messengers in their languages, so We have sent down to you the Book as a judgment in Arabic.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ in the religion. It was also said: in the qibla, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector (wali) or defender (waqi) against Allah.﴾ That is: no helper (nasir) and no guardian (hafiz).

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We did send messengers before you⦆ It is related that the Jews – and it was also said that the polytheists – said: "This man has no concern except for women." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And We did send messengers before you and We gave them wives and offspring﴾ [[Narrated by al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 317, from al-Kalbi without an isnad. See also: Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/327; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 5/397.]] and We did not make them angels who do not eat, drink or marry.

It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it, its implied meaning being: for every Book there is a term and a period, i.e., the revealed Books each have a time at which it descends.
